articles.title: SJAA EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document is the November 1994 issue (Volume 5, Number 8) of the "SJAA EPHEMERIS," the official publication of the San Jose Astronomical Association. It serves as a regular communication for members of the astronomy club.

articles.title: The Eyepiece
articles.summary: This issue of 'The Eyepiece' highlights editor Bob Madden's concerns over low member article submissions, leading to discussions about potentially reducing the publication's size and increasing membership dues to support the Observatory Fund. The document also provides a comprehensive calendar of November and December events, including various star parties and general meetings featuring speakers on topics like Pluto and the Jupiter/SL9 collisions. Furthermore, it includes a review of the 'Redscope' astronomical software, detailing its features for calculating telescope parameters.

articles.title: RedShift (continued from page 1)
articles.summary: This article reviews 'RedShift' (also referred to as 'Redscope') software, designed for amateur astronomers to simulate observing conditions and equipment performance. It allows users to conduct 'thought experiments' with various telescope, eyepiece, and filter combinations, helping them plan future equipment purchases or optimize existing setups from the comfort of their home. The program, currently PC-only, is praised for its affordability and extensive features, including data on numerous commercially available eyepieces and a detailed glossary.

articles.title: S-80 test report from Yosemite by timmyd@netcom.com (Tim DeBenedictis)
articles.summary: This report details Tim DeBenedictis's purchase and field test of an S-80 spotting scope, along with a Velbon DH-10ML tripod and an Orion slow-motion control, for backpacking astronomy. He reviews the equipment, praising Pocono Mountain Optics' service, and recounts a demanding hike to Clouds' Rest in Yosemite. The S-80 performed well for terrestrial observations of Half Dome but showed only an "unimpressive smudge" for the Andromeda galaxy under initial hazy conditions, though the sky cleared later.

articles.title: Yosemite (continued from page 2
articles.summary: An amateur astronomer recounts an exceptional stargazing experience from 10,000 feet on Clouds' Rest in Yosemite. The incredibly dark sky allowed for spectacular naked-eye views of the Milky Way, Andromeda galaxy, and numerous Pleiads, while an 80mm spotting scope revealed fine details in deep-sky objects like dust lanes in Andromeda, split double stars, and even the faint Crab Nebula. The report highlights the clarity of the high-altitude sky and the performance of the equipment, despite minor observational discomforts.

articles.title: DISCOVERY GAUGES SIZE AND AGE OF THE UNIVERSE
articles.summary: Astronomers using the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope have discovered Cepheid variable stars in the distant Virgo Cluster, resolving a decades-long debate about the universe's distance scale. This discovery sets the Virgo Cluster at 50 million Light Years away, implying that remote cosmic objects are closer than previously thought, and leads to a revised Hubble Constant. The new measurements suggest the universe is 7-11 billion years old, creating a paradox with the estimated age of the oldest stars (16 billion years) which challenges current cosmological models.

articles.title: AGE (continued from page 3)
articles.summary: This article discusses the use of Cepheid variable stars as a reliable tool for estimating cosmological distances, particularly in the Virgo Cluster. It highlights the crucial role of the High Resolution Camera (HRCam) on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, which produces sharper images by correcting for atmospheric turbulence. The work of Dr. McClure, Dr. Racine, and Dr. Stetson in developing the HRCam and its analysis software, respectively, was recognized with prestigious astronomical awards.

articles.title: For More Information:
articles.summary: This document provides contact information for several prominent astronomers from various universities and observatories. It also includes an email from 1994, posted to a scientific newsgroup, questioning the validity and media hype surrounding a press release on new determinations of the universe's size and age. The sender specifically asks for clarification on a reported Hubble Constant (H_0) value and its implications for globular cluster ages, seeking to understand if the scientific controversy has been settled.

articles.title: Bram Boroson
articles.summary: Ethan Bradford discusses a press release concerning the universe's size and age, specifically addressing a reported Hubble Constant (H_0) of 88 km/s/Mpc. He argues this value is higher than many recent estimates and exacerbates the 'age problem' related to globular clusters. While Cepheid observations support a higher H_0, Bradford contends the controversy isn't settled due to unaddressed systematic errors, though he anticipates a resolution within a few years.

articles.title: What Have You Seen Lately From: strong@uoport.edu (Caroline Strong)
articles.summary: This document is a newsgroup post from Caroline Strong on October 3, 1994, to sci.astro.amateur. It appears to be an observing report or a query about recent observations, specifically mentioning the Horsehead Nebula.

articles.title: Juniper Sky Ranch Sept 30-Oct 1:
articles.summary: An amateur astronomy enthusiast details a successful observing weekend at Juniper Sky Ranch, highlighted by exceptional views of various deep-sky objects including the Veil Nebula, Crescent Nebula, and a first-time clear sighting of the Horsehead Nebula with an H-beta filter. The report also covers a daytime trip to scout potential sites for the 1995 Oregon Star Party, including a visit to Pine Mountain Observatory.

articles.title: Whatcha been looking at lately? From: jackz@sxzi.hp.com (Jack Zeiders)
articles.summary: This article is a discussion among amateur astronomers sharing their recent celestial observations and favorite deep-sky objects. Participants describe various nebulae, galaxies, and star clusters, often mentioning specific NGC numbers, magnitudes, and useful filters like OIII and UHC. The conversation also includes tips on magnification and observing conditions for different objects.

articles.title: Mounting Rings Made Easy by Paul Barton
articles.summary: This article describes a simple DIY method for creating mounting rings for an Optical Tube Assembly (OTA) or finder scope using thick-walled PVC pipe. The process involves cutting the PVC pipe to width, slitting it, heating it in an oven until soft, and then shaping it around the OTA or a form until cool. The finished ring can then be lined with felt and attached to an equatorial mount.

articles.title: Observational Astronomy Class
articles.summary: This document outlines information for an Observational Astronomy Class, indicating several instances of 'no meeting' and listing a series of numbers without explicit context. A critical instruction advises participants to consult their Ephemeris monthly for any schedule or content changes.

articles.title: Telescope Loaner Status
articles.summary: This document from the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) details the current status of its telescope loaner program for members. It lists various telescopes, indicating which are currently borrowed, by whom, and their respective due dates, with several units marked as available. The article also provides instructions for members on how to borrow a telescope by contacting Paul Barton to be added to a waiting list, noting a special solar telescope available for experienced members.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: ASTRO ADS offers free classified advertisements for non-commercial astronomy-related products and services. Ads must be submitted to the editor by the 12th of each month and typically run for three months. The document includes examples of ads for various astronomical equipment such as telescopes, mounts, flats, and mirror blanks.

articles.title: November 1994
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical almanac for November 1994, detailing lunar phases, rise, transit, and set times for the Moon and five nearer planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn). It also includes solar data, astronomical twilight times, sidereal time, and highlights the 'Darkest Saturday Night' of the month. All presented times and dates are in Pacific Standard.

articles.title: Offices and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current Officers and Board of Directors of an organization, detailing their names, positions (President, Vice President, Secretary, Treasurer, and Director), and contact phone numbers. It serves as a directory for the organization's leadership.

articles.title: Ephemeris Contributors
articles.summary: This document provides contact information for individuals involved in the production and distribution of an ephemeris. It lists Don Machholz and Paul Barton as contributors, with Bob Madden serving as the editor. Paul Barton and Bob Madden are also responsible for the distribution.

articles.title: Comet Comments
articles.summary: Don Machholz's "Comet Comments" provides updates on several comets, detailing the recent recovery of one and the ongoing observations of Periodic Comet Machholz 2 (1994o), noting its dimming and a companion's brief brightening. The article also reports on fragments breaking off Periodic Comet Harrington (1994g) and the recovery of Periodic Comet Reimuth 1 (1994p). It concludes with detailed ephemerides for Periodic Comet Borrelly (1994i) and Machholz 2 (1994o), alongside orbital elements for the latter.

articles.title: SAN JOSE ASTRONOMICAL ASSOCIATION MEMBERSHIP
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) publishes a monthly newsletter called "EPHEMERIS" and actively encourages its members to submit articles for publication. Submissions must be typed, sent to editor Bob Madden by the 17th of the previous month, and are preferred as a text file on a 3-1/2" diskette, though written submissions are also accepted.

articles.title: Membership only: $12 Membership / S&T: $32 Junior (under 18): $20
articles.summary: This document is a membership application form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), detailing various membership tiers: $12 for basic, $32 including a Sky & Telescope subscription, and $20 for juniors. It provides fields for personal information and instructions for submitting the form and payment to the SJAA treasurer.
